title: Eg-walker merges edits in milliseconds
excerpt: Eg-walker turns a one-hour Git Makefile merge into a 24 ms operation by using a throwaway CRDT.
body:
## A real-world merge that blew the mind  

A recent EuroSys 2025 paper measured the time it takes to merge the full edit history of Git’s own Makefile. Merging that history with a classic Operational Transformation (OT) algorithm runs for about one hour. The same history merged with the Eg-walker algorithm finishes in 24 milliseconds. The dramatic speedup comes from a single change: replicas store a directed-acyclic graph (DAG) of edits instead of a full CRDT state.  

Each event in the graph holds three pieces of data, an identifier, the identifiers of its parent events, and the raw operation exactly as the user performed it. Because the graph records precisely what each author saw, replaying it deterministically reproduces the document on any replica. The paper describes this as “store the history, not the state” and defines the document as  

```text
document = replay(eventGraph)
```  

[[source]](https://dev.to/james_anderson_h/the-crdt-that-throws-itself-away-inside-eg-walker-1bn0).  

The reader will learn why traditional approaches struggle, how Eg-walker flips the storage model, and what concrete steps a collaborative editor can take to get fast, lightweight merges.  

## Why traditional approaches struggle  

Two families of algorithms dominate collaborative text editing. Operational Transformation stores the document as plain text and transforms every incoming operation against all previous ones.

When two users each make *n* edits while offline, each edit from one side must be transformed against every edit from the other side, giving at least *O(n²)* work; some OT variants are cubic or worse. The approach works well for real-time typing with small edit bursts, but it becomes painful for offline work or long-running branches.

Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) assign a unique identifier to every character and store positions relative to those identifiers. Merging long branches is cheap and the algorithm works peer-to-peer, but the metadata required to track identifiers uses more than ten times the memory of OT, according to the paper. The heavy metadata must be loaded from disk and kept in memory for the entire session, even when nobody else is editing.  

In practice, developers end up choosing between slow merges (OT) and heavyweight documents (CRDTs).  

## Storing the history instead of the state  

Eg-walker flips the usual storage model. Rather than persisting per-character identifiers, each replica keeps an event graph, a DAG where every node records the raw edit operation. The graph’s edges capture the parent events that the author had seen when the edit was made. Two events are concurrent if neither is an ancestor of the other, just like two commits on different branches in Git.  

With this representation the document is defined as a pure function of the event graph. The `replay` function walks the graph in topological order and applies each raw operation to a plain string. Because the operation is stored exactly as the user typed it (for example `Insert(3, "l")` or `Delete(1)`), no transformation is required during replay. The approach mirrors Git’s model of commits and merges, which makes the concept easy to reason about for anyone familiar with version control.  

## Building a CRDT only when concurrency appears  

The key insight behind Eg-walker is that a full CRDT is needed only when concurrent edits must be merged. Most real-world editing histories are largely sequential: authors take turns, or a single author works alone for long periods. When an edit arrives whose parent is the current document state, its index is already correct and can be applied directly to the plain string. No transformation or metadata lookup is necessary.  

Eg-walker therefore keeps three items per replica:

1. The document as plain text, held in memory with no per-character metadata.  
2. A temporary CRDT state that is constructed only when concurrent events need merging. This state lives in memory for the duration of the merge and is never persisted to disk or sent over the network.  
3. The event graph, which is the persistent representation of the edit history.  

When concurrency is detected, Eg-walker walks the event graph in topological order and builds the temporary CRDT on the fly. The algorithm tracks two versions of the document simultaneously. The *effect version* is the document after applying all events processed so far and only moves forward. The *prepare version* is the document exactly as the author of the current event saw it; it may move backward and forward to match the author’s view.  

A deletion operation refers to an index in the author’s view, not the current effect version. By rewinding the prepare version to the author’s snapshot, applying the delete, and then advancing the effect version, the algorithm preserves the intended semantics without needing permanent identifiers.  

## Linear-time merges and tiny memory footprints  

Because the temporary CRDT is built once per merge and discarded immediately afterward, the memory overhead stays low. The merge itself runs in linear time over the number of events in the graph, avoiding the quadratic blow-up that plagues OT. The paper’s measurement, merging the Makefile history in 24 milliseconds, demonstrates that the approach scales to real-world edit histories while keeping the persistent state lightweight.  

## The takeaway  

Eg-walker shows that persisting an event graph and constructing a CRDT only when concurrent edits need resolution can shrink merge times from hours to milliseconds and keep memory usage close to that of a plain-text document.

For collaborative editors, the practical recipe is to store the raw edit history as a DAG, keep the live document as plain text, and treat the CRDT as a short-lived helper during merges. This strategy delivers fast, lightweight merges without the heavy metadata burden of traditional CRDT implementations.
